title: 1 Chronicles 12:16–22
context: Men of Benjamin and Judah come to David’s stronghold. David meets them cautiously, offering a united heart if they come in peace and calling on God to judge if they come to betray him. The Spirit comes on Amasai, chief of the thirty, who declares loyalty to David and peace on him and his helpers, for God helps him; David makes them captains. Men of Manasseh also join David when the Philistine lords send him away from the battle against Saul (compare 1 Samuel 29), and they help him against a band of raiders (compare 1 Samuel 30). Day by day men come until David has a great army.

verses.text: Some of the children of Benjamin and Judah came to the stronghold to David.
verses.arminianNotes: Men of Benjamin and Judah come to David at the stronghold. Arminian readers note that support now comes from both Saul’s tribe and David’s own, a sign of growing unity around him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God drawing together tribes that would later be united under David. Both traditions read the verse as introducing a tense encounter, as David must judge whether these men come in good faith.

verses.text: David went out to meet them, and answered them, “If you have come peaceably to me to help me, my heart will be united with you; but if you have come to betray me to my adversaries, since there is no wrong in my hands, may the God of our fathers see this and rebuke it.”
verses.arminianNotes: David offers a united heart if they come in peace, but calls on God to see and rebuke betrayal. Arminian readers note his caution and his appeal to God’s justice, since he had been betrayed before.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David entrusting judgment to God rather than acting on suspicion alone. Shared ground: David’s words show both openness and wisdom, and both traditions read them as a model of discerning leadership.

verses.text: Then the Spirit came on Amasai, who was chief of the thirty, and he said, “We are yours, David, and on your side, you son of Jesse. Peace, peace be to you, and peace be to your helpers; for your God helps you.” Then David received them and made them captains of the band.
verses.arminianNotes: The Spirit comes on Amasai, chief of the thirty, who pledges loyalty and peace to David, for God helps him. Arminian readers see the Spirit prompting a public declaration of allegiance at a decisive moment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Spirit confirming God’s choice of David through Amasai’s words. Shared ground: both traditions read the Spirit’s coming here as empowering a specific word; some link Amasai with Amasa (2 Samuel 17:25), but this is uncertain.

verses.text: Some of Manasseh also joined David when he came with the Philistines against Saul to battle, but they didn’t help them, for the lords of the Philistines sent him away after consultation, saying, “He will desert to his master Saul to the jeopardy of our heads.”
verses.arminianNotes: Some of Manasseh join David when he goes with the Philistines against Saul, but the Philistine lords send him away. Arminian readers note that the account recalls 1 Samuel 29, where David is dismissed from the battle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providence sparing David from fighting against Israel. Both traditions read the verse as parallel to 1 Samuel 29:1–11 by reference, with the Philistine lords’ fear of desertion recorded here as well.

verses.text: As he went to Ziklag, some from Manasseh joined him: Adnah, Jozabad, Jediael, Michael, Jozabad, Elihu, and Zillethai, captains of thousands who were of Manasseh.
verses.arminianNotes: As David returns to Ziklag, Manassite captains of thousands join him. Arminian readers note that seven named leaders from Manasseh come to David at a critical moment, just before the crisis at Ziklag.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see support arriving at the right time, as part of God’s provision. Shared ground: the repeated name Jozabad shows that two men shared a name, and both traditions read the list as historical record.

verses.text: They helped David against the band of raiders, for they were all mighty men of valor and were captains in the army.
verses.arminianNotes: They help David against the band of raiders, being mighty men of valor. Arminian readers note that this likely refers to the Amalekite raid on Ziklag in 1 Samuel 30, though the verse does not name the raiders.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see these men as part of the means by which God enabled David to recover what was lost. Both traditions read the verse as connecting the list to events narrated in 1 Samuel 30, without claiming more than it says.

verses.text: For from day to day men came to David to help him, until there was a great army, like God’s army.
verses.arminianNotes: Day by day men come to David until there is a great army, like God’s army. Arminian readers note that the growth happens through many individual decisions to join David over time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the phrase “like God’s army” as an idiom for something very great, pointing to God’s blessing on David. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as summarizing the steady growth of David’s support.
